tagline: Japan's calmest sea, its most famous art islands — and a million art-pilgrims a year still crossing on slow scheduled ferries.
summary: The Seto Inland Sea is the structurally calmest large body of water in Japan: a sheltered, almost lake-like sea threaded with hundreds of islands between Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu — close to ideal foiling water. It already carries one of the world's densest small-craft networks, linking the Benesse art islands (Naoshima, Teshima, Inujima), Miyajima/Itsukushima, and the gateway ports of Takamatsu, Onomichi and Hiroshima. The Setouchi Triennale alone pulls ~1 million visitors onto these crossings, yet every hop is a fixed-schedule diesel ferry. This is a mature, adopted island-hopping habit waiting to be modernised, not a market that has to be created.

demand_signals.label: Setouchi Triennale attendance
demand_signals.note: Triennial art festival across Naoshima/Teshima/Inujima and ~12 islands; every visitor moves island-to-island by boat. Next editions 2025/2028.

demand_signals.label: Miyajima / Itsukushima visitors
demand_signals.note: UNESCO World Heritage island shrine; reached only by ferry from Miyajimaguchi. A 100-yen visitor levy is now collected via the ferry fare.

demand_signals.label: Calmest water body in Japan
demand_signals.note: Setonaikai National Park — Japan's first national park (1934); protected, low-swell water that is close to ideal for hydrofoiling.

demand_signals.label: Premium hospitality pipeline
demand_signals.note: Concentration of design-led luxury hotels and the Benesse Art Site portfolio across multiple islands — high-value guests on undifferentiated public ferries.

demand_signals.label: Ferry-only inter-island access
demand_signals.note: Art-island hops (Takamatsu/Uno ↔ Naoshima ↔ Teshima ↔ Inujima) all run on conventional scheduled ferries — no on-demand, no premium, no clean option.

use_cases.title: Art-island hopping on demand
use_cases.body: A smooth, near-silent foiling shuttle linking Takamatsu/Uno, Naoshima, Teshima and Inujima lets Triennale and year-round art visitors move on their own schedule instead of clustering around sparse ferry departures — turning the journey between artworks into part of the experience.

use_cases.title: Hotel-to-island private transfers
use_cases.body: Direct foiling arrivals to island and hotel jetties (Benesse, Aman/Janu pipeline, Hoshinoya) replace the public-ferry-plus-shuttle chain with one seamless premium hop across glassy protected water.

use_cases.title: Hiroshima ↔ Miyajima clean crossing
use_cases.body: A high-frequency all-electric crossing for the ~4.6M/yr Miyajima flow — zero-emission service into the waters of a UNESCO World Heritage shrine island and Setonaikai National Park.

use_cases.title: Gateway-port commuter mesh
use_cases.body: Takamatsu, Onomichi, Uno and Hiroshima anchor a dense web of short inter-island hops that today depend on weather-exposed conventional craft — a natural backbone for a clean, reliable scheduled foiling network.

journeys.today: Scheduled diesel ferry or fast boat; you plan your day around the timetable and queue at peak Triennale periods.
journeys.with_navier: An on-demand, near-silent foiling hop across calm water — arrive on your schedule, glide straight to the island jetty.

journeys.today: Sparse inter-island ferries; missing one connection can cost hours and force a backtrack through a hub port.
journeys.with_navier: A direct island-to-island foiling chain that strings the three art islands together in minutes, on demand.

journeys.today: Tram or train to Miyajimaguchi, then a crowded diesel ferry; or a limited direct sightseeing boat.
journeys.with_navier: A direct, zero-emission foiling crossing from central Hiroshima to the shrine island — fast, smooth and clean in protected waters.

journeys.today: No fast direct boat; travellers loop inland by train via Okayama.
journeys.with_navier: A long protected-water line-haul across the Inland Sea linking two gateway cities directly — hybrid range with no charging stop.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: Nearly the entire network is Pioneer II territory: art-island hops (Takamatsu/Uno ↔ Naoshima ↔ Teshima ↔ Inujima), Hiroshima ↔ Miyajima (~11 nm) and the Onomichi/Shimanami island chain all sit comfortably inside the 70 nm all-electric envelope on the calmest water in Japan — ideal for multiple daily rotations.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Long cross-sea line-hauls between the gateway cities — e.g. Takamatsu (Shikoku) ↔ Hiroshima (Honshu) at roughly 80 nm — exceed the all-electric range and are the Quanta-LR corridors, knitting the seven-prefecture Inland Sea into one continuous network without any new charging infrastructure.

competitive_landscape: The Inland Sea is served today by a dense patchwork of conventional ferry and fast-boat operators (JR-West Miyajima ferry, Shikoku Kisen and the Naoshima art-island lines, the Setouchi Triennale charter boats, plus dozens of municipal routes). The volume proves the demand — roughly a million Triennale visitors and ~4.6M Miyajima arrivals a year — but the experience is fixed-schedule, diesel, and undifferentiated. Premium hospitality guests and art pilgrims alike ride the same public timetable. That gap between world-class destinations and commodity transport is precisely the opening.

precedents.what: Japan already accepts fast above-water craft
precedents.where: Tokai Kisen jetfoils, Tokyo ↔ Izu Islands
precedents.why_it_matters: Decades of high-speed foil-borne ferry service in Japan mean passengers already understand and value flying above the chop — the modern, clean, quiet evolution is an easy step, not a new behaviour.
A $100M, ~100-vessel phased electric-foiling network shows the model works at national scale — a playbook to replicate for an archipelago tourism economy like Setouchi.

seasonality: The Seto Inland Sea is the most sheltered large water body in Japan — low swell and minimal fetch year-round, which is why it is close to ideal foiling water. The main exposure is the late-summer typhoon window (roughly Aug–Sep), when even the calm sea can see brief disruption; outside that, conditions are benign and foiling's smooth, near-silent ride is a comfort upgrade on every crossing.
regulatory_note: Operates under Japan Coast Guard (JCG) and MLIT Maritime Bureau safety oversight. The entire region lies within Setonaikai National Park (Japan's first, 1934) and includes UNESCO World Heritage Itsukushima — a strong clean-marine mandate where replacing diesel ferry emissions in protected, heavily-visited waters is concrete demand evidence. Aligns with Japan's 2050 carbon-neutrality and MLIT zero-emission-vessel programmes.
signature_routes: Takamatsu / Uno ↔ Naoshima ↔ Teshima ↔ Inujima (art-island foiling chain, all-electric)
